ally-aiken.name: Ally Aiken Design
ally-aiken.line: Watercolour golf course maps from Austin — hundreds of courses, commissions open.
src: The good Texas golf brands are makers rather than marketers — a silversmith, a knitter, a pair of machine shops — which is the reason to run them together. The bar is narrow on purpose: founded in Texas, and still based in Texas. That cuts the brands putting a longhorn on a hat from an office in California, and it cuts the companies that opened a Dallas warehouse and started calling themselves Texan.

Sixteen clear it, and they have startlingly little in common. Clint Orms has been hand-engraving silver in Kerrville since 1992 and will not reproduce more than ten pieces from any one design. Ally Aiken painted a course map for her husband in 2020 and now has hundreds of courses in the catalogue. Harry and Zach wrap leather grips in Conroe as a father-and-son shop, Scott Matthews left investment banking in New York for Dallas over a polyester polo, and Mike Taylor and John Hatfield came off the Nike payroll on a Friday and opened Artisan in the same Fort Worth building on the Monday.

That last one is the closest thing to a pattern. When Nike left the golf equipment business in 2016 it left behind a ten-thousand-square-foot building in Fort Worth and a group of people who knew how to grind a wedge, and two of the best club shops in the country grew out of the vacancy. P53 leases its space in that same building from Marty Leonard, whose father Marvin built Colonial. Ben Hogan is buried in the city. The metal work clusters where it does for a reason.

One distinction matters in the apparel section: designed in Texas and made in Texas are not the same claim. Criquet designs at its Clubhouse in Austin and prints made in Peru on the Players Shirt. Artisan prints made in Fort Worth on the building. Both are fine, and the good ones say which is which on the product page.

apc-golf.name: A.P.C. Golf
apc-golf.line: Jean Touitou's golf line, launched in Korea and Japan first. Collaborated with Cph/Golf, 2026.
src: The two marks do not sit side by side on these eighteen pieces. They have been welded into one, A.P.Cph , embroidered or printed on the chest of nearly everything A.P.C. Golf and Tokyo's Cph/Golf released together this morning. Prices run 4,400 to 28,600, or roughly $28 to $179, with the no-collar jacket at the top of the range and a two-pack of socks at the bottom.

The graphics do the arguing. Several tops carry 39 RUE MADAME PARIS across the back — A.P.C.'s head office in the 6th, with its Paris store across the road at 38 — transplanted onto Japanese golf wear. The half zip goes one better and runs that address against Cph/Golf's own house line, NOT A GOLF GENTLEMAN . Everything sits in black, navy, white, cream and light grey, with navy doing the colour-blocking.

It is aimed at the golfer who dresses for the parking lot as much as the first tee, which both labels have been serving for years from opposite ends of the world. The complication is geography: this is a Japan-only release on a Japan-only store, and six of the eighteen sold out on day one. What follows is every piece, what it costs in dollars, and the honest options for getting one from the States.

Six tops and one jacket, all cut with the roomy shoulder and slightly cropped body Cph/Golf uses across its own range. Every reference is sized M to XL against a 183cm fit model in L, so the cm charts matter more than the letter.

apres-golf.name: Après Golf
apres-golf.line: Hi-loft sherpa fleece headcovers hand-sewn in California, with vintage ski-resort and country-club patches sewn on top.
src: Apr s Golf makes hi-loft sherpa fleece headcovers, hand-sewn in California, and sews vintage patches onto them — ski resorts, country clubs, and whatever else turns up. Fifty pieces are below, across eight groups, all of them in stock on 9 September 2026.

The idea starts with the name. Apr s-ski is the part of a ski day that happens after the skiing, and the patches that end up on these covers came off ski jackets: Chamonix, St. Moritz, Alta, Mad River Glen. Apr s buys them, cuts fleece around them, and sells the result to golfers. The brand describes what it does plainly on its own site — "We source vintage patches, create new patches, embroider logos and print custom designs." The sewing happens in a California factory that has been running since 1992, at a mill that also supplies fleece to outdoor and fashion labels.

If you want the short version: the tie-dye prints are the ones people stop you about, the vintage patches are the ones that will not be repeatable, and the whole catalogue is really an advertisement for the custom programme, where you post them a patch of your own.
Apr s prints and dyes its own fleece, and this is the part of the catalogue that looks like nothing else on a first tee.

aug-11.name: Aug 11
aug-11.line: Hat brand founded in 2023 by Johnny Person — rope caps and buckets with a vintage Southern lean.
src: Aug 11 isn't a golf brand. It's a hat brand. But the best hats on the course right now aren't coming from golf companies — they're crossing over from streetwear, from lifestyle, from places where fit and story matter more than a logo on a divot tool. Aug 11 is that brand.

Founded in 2023 by Johnny Person out of Atlanta, the name comes from his little sister Isabell's birthday — August 11, 2003. In late 2010, Johnny was homeless and battling addiction. His sister told him the truth: he was hurting her. That conversation became the turning point. Every hat in the line carries a name tied to that arc — "Lord Forgive Me," "Loverboy," "Art" — and the brand's tagline is "Unbreakable Resilience." It's not marketing. It's the actual story.

Before you dismiss it as another DTC hat company, look at who's wearing them. Aaron Judge. Jrue Holiday. Dom Dolla wore Aug 11 to three of his four Coachella sets. Adam Mosseri — the head of Instagram — posted in one to his 2.4 million followers. None of that was paid. The hats just fit well and look right, and people with platforms noticed.

The line is mostly structured snapbacks, unstructured dad hats, mesh truckers, and felt hats — all $54.95, with the felt at $59.95. The quality-to-price ratio is aggressive. Johnny grew up down the street from Hurley, Volcom, and Quiksilver in Costa Mesa and spent a decade in the apparel industry before launching. He knows how a hat should sit on your head, and it shows. Ten pieces here. All of them course-ready.

beams-golf.name: BEAMS Golf
beams-golf.line: The golf line of Tokyo's BEAMS empire, running since 2011 — Japanese fairway fashion at its most complete.
src: In 1976, a guy named Etsuzo Shitara opened a 21.5 square meter shop in Harajuku called "American Life Shop BEAMS." Styled like a UCLA dorm room, stocked with early Nike running sneakers and West Coast campus wear his partner bought on trips to California with enormous empty bags. Fifty years later, BEAMS operates 160 stores with 50 sub-labels and is considered, in Nigo's words, "the very pinnacle of Tokyo culture." In 2011, they turned that editorial eye to golf — and created Japan's first select-shop golf brand.

The man behind it is Satoshi Nishiwaki, who joined BEAMS as a part-timer in 1995 and had never played golf before directing the brand. That turned out to be the point. BEAMS Golf doesn't start from performance and add style. It starts from fashion identity and engineers performance into it. Three sub-labels cover the range: Orange Label for American-casual boldness, Purple Label for modernized tradition, and B.G.THREE for minimalist city-to-course crossover. In 2019, a 20-year-old rookie named Hinako Shibuno wore BEAMS Golf Orange Label to win the AIG Women's British Open — her first tournament outside Japan. The polo sold out within hours. BEAMS issued a victory commemorative edition four days later.

The collaboration list reads like a who's-who of taste: Malbon Golf, Polo Ralph Lauren, BRIEFING, Hender Scheme, SON OF THE CHEESE, Nike Golf, Jones Sports Co . Fifteen collaborations deep with Ralph Lauren alone. The catch is getting it stateside — BEAMS ships internationally through WorldShopping, Buyee handles proxy orders, and the occasional Malbon or FARFETCH drop crosses the Pacific. That barrier is part of the appeal. You won't see it at the local muni. You'll know who did their homework.

BEAMS Golf launched in spring 2011 as Japan’s first select-shop golf brand. It is the golf arm of BEAMS Co., Ltd., the Tokyo retailer founded in 1976 that now operates around 160 stores and 50 sub-labels.

big-dog-golf.name: Big Dog Golf Co.
big-dog-golf.line: Leather covers stocked in the pro shops at Royal Melbourne, Barnbougle and Cape Wickham.
src: Australia is the best golf destination almost no American has been to, and the problem is information rather than distance. Half of what gets written about the Melbourne Sandbelt in the US repeats a myth about Alister MacKenzie designing all of it, and almost none of it tells you what a trip costs or how you get on one.

Two things are going on down there. The independent apparel and leather brands have got very good very fast, and nobody outside Australia is covering them properly. Alongside them sits a small set of organised trips an American can book, with prices exactly as published and a clear note where an operator publishes none.

Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip, and no other golf media or apparel brand in the world does. The rest of the field sits it out: No Laying Up, Fried Egg, The Golfer's Journal, Bob Does Sports, Good Good, Skratch, and a dozen clothing labels from Manors to Malbon to Eastside. Fried Egg has a deposit system and a calendar published a year ahead, and points its entire international programme at Britain and Ireland. That leaves a hole in the market, and for now one fourteen-person van tour is filling it.

Brand prices are in Australian dollars, because that is what these businesses charge. At late-August 2026 rates an Australian dollar is about seventy-two US cents, so knock off a bit under a third. Trip prices are quoted in whatever currency the operator publishes, and each one is labelled. Where an operator publishes no price at all, that is noted rather than guessed at.

birds-of-condor.name: Birds of Condor
birds-of-condor.line: Byron Bay's cult label — started with ten hats, now a flagship store with a restored 80s buggy inside.
src: Frankie Kimpton booked bands for Mushroom in Melbourne before he made golf hats. He grew up surfing competitively in Byron Bay, and golf was the thing he and his mates did when there were no waves. When he started turning up at driving ranges more often, he did not fit, and he has been unusually direct about why.

He and Zoe Kimpton, his wife and co-founder, started with ten hats out of a garage. The brand dates itself to 2016, from an idea that began on Melbourne driving-range lunch breaks around 2013 and 2014. Within months it was shipping to South Korea, Japan and the United States. It now has roughly 128 stockists across Australia and New Zealand, and the split is the whole story: about half are golf clubs and driving ranges, and about half are surf and skate shops — Culture Kings, Stateside Sports, Hillzeez. In November 2025 they opened a first flagship on Lawson Street in Byron Bay, with a restored 1980s golf buggy in the fit-out.

A birdie is one under on a hole. An eagle is two. An albatross is three. A condor is four — a hole in one on a par five — and in the brand's own words on its About page, it is "the rarest event in golf. Only a handful ever recorded, none of which have occurred in professional golf. It's also known as a Triple Eagle and is what our logo represents." That last part is literal: the mark stacks three W-shaped eagles.

bluegrass-fairway.name: Bluegrass Fairway
bluegrass-fairway.line: Handmade leather, Harris Tweed and waxed canvas golf goods, made in Louisville since 2015.
src: Bluegrass Fairway is a small workshop in Louisville, Kentucky making leather, Harris Tweed and waxed canvas golf goods by hand — headcovers, yardage book covers, valuables pouches, rangefinder cases and the occasional needlepoint belt. Around 172 products are live at any one time, priced from about $38 for a hat to $1,100 for a bag built out of a repurposed Barbour jacket.

The company exists because a cheap yardage book cover fell apart. Matt Reynolds took it to a local shoe cobbler to be repaired, and the cobbler told him they could simply build a better one. They went through roughly three versions. Friends asked for copies, a friend's wife suggested Etsy, and in October 2015 he listed it. One sale came in the first month. Then about a hundred arrived over the next forty days, and the cobbler could not keep up.

For anyone who likes the idea of golf equipment made from named materials by identifiable people, this is a straightforward recommendation. It is also cheaper to get into than that description implies: a Horween scorecard holder is $85, and a waxed canvas headcover is $100.
Reynolds has given two published interviews, both in 2017. The quotes below are from those, and are dated accordingly.

bluetross.name: Bluetross
bluetross.line: Horween and Italian leather covers, belts and wallets, co-founded by Gail Hanson.
src: The argument for this group is not who founded the brands but how well the things are made, and Jan Craig is the proof. In 1962 a golfer of that name, out on a rural route outside Cincinnati, made her own headcovers in worsted wool because she could not buy any she liked for a new set of clubs. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set within a few years, Tom Watson carried them, and so did multiple Ryder Cup teams. Every cover is still hand-knit to order, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver.

The animal headcover came seventeen years later, from a mother and daughter in Phoenix. Frank, the tiger, went on Tiger Woods' driver at the 1997 Masters, Nike licensed the character and named him, and the business grew four hundred per cent in a quarter.

Neither of those is a novelty company, and neither is interesting only for who started it. Seventeen brands do both things at once: founded or co-founded by a woman, and making what men buy, which is headcovers, leather, bags, gloves, towels, socks, polos and shoes. Almost every women-founded golf brand makes women's apparel and nothing else, and almost every independent brand making unisex hard goods was founded by men, so the overlap between the two runs thin.

One pattern turns up again and again. Megan Chisti co-founded Seamus, trained as the designer, rebuilt the headcover that started the company and still sews product, and there is no published quote from her anywhere. Gail Hanson co-founded Bluetross, and the first prototypes came off her inherited sewing machine; the biggest feature ever written about the company is headlined "the unlikely story of a man who quit his job to make leather headcovers." Neither brand is hiding anything, and both credit her plainly on their own About page. The voice just defaults to him. So every entry names the woman, and says plainly when she co-founded with a husband or a mother rather than rounding up.

casualist.line: Elie Reboul's West London label that outgrew its own name — quiet clothes for golf and after.
src: The best-selling item Casualist makes has the wrong name on it. The Casual Pro Snapback is the oldest thing in the catalogue, it restocked this month, and stitched across the front is CASUAL PRO, SINCE 2023, LEISURE APPAREL, MELB LDN LA. That was the brand before this one.

Elie Reboul renamed it. His explanation, on the about page, is two sentences long: the spirit was right, but the name needed to grow up a little. Casualist is the version with sharper details and a clearer point of view. What he did not do is retire the old hat, and the archive section still sells a navy coach jacket with CASUAL PRO in block type across the back.

The brand is West London. It says so on the Two Tone Course Cap, under the words Leisure Goods. Everything is designed there and most of it is made in Portugal, with fabric chosen for how it feels after eighteen holes rather than how it reads on a screen. The test they apply to anything before making it is whether they would wear it properly and repeatedly, not once and not for the photos.

Seventeen products. Polos with collars soft enough to pack, tees that carry the jokes, a cardigan vest meant sincerely for a drizzly Tuesday, pleated trousers cut closer to trousers than to golf pants. And, at the bottom of the catalogue, a 12,000 electric golf cart in cream with a striped canopy.

cloud-and-wind-golf.line: Grips only — Eastern aesthetics, Chinese verse printed on the box, $18 a grip.
src: Cloud & Wind Golf makes one thing — grips — and they make them differently. Every design draws from traditional Eastern aesthetics and Pacific Coast nature. The Blossom series pulls from floral motifs and Chinese poetry. The Cloud & Wave collection captures the mood of twilight rounds on the California coast. The Zen strips everything back to texture and tone. Each grip ships with a line of Chinese verse printed along the shaft — a detail most brands would never think to include.

The construction is straightforward: natural and synthetic rubber blend, Standard+ sizing with a gentle taper, 56–58 grams, rated for 60 rounds. At $18 a grip, they're priced below the big names but built with more intention than anything in the pro shop. Bundles drop the per-grip cost further — a 3-grip set runs $50, a 7-grip set is $112. The new Pacific Summer collection just landed with three colorways inspired by June Gloom mornings and SoCal sunsets. This is a grip brand for golfers who care about what they touch 50+ times a round.

criquet.line: Austin's original players shirt, est. 2010 — Pima cotton, removable stays, made in Peru and says so.
src: Criquet makes golf shirts that never announce themselves as golf shirts, which is how the same four-button placket ends up on a Butler tee box and at a South Congress bar three hours later. Billy Nachman and Hobson Brown have known each other since kindergarten in Manhattan, where they grew up in prep-school polos and coat-and-tie dress codes, and they started the company in Austin in 2010. It begins in a closet, with the vintage golf shirt Nachman's grandfather left behind: four buttons, a long placket, a collar that had opinions. They rebuilt it with a flap chest pocket, removable collar stays so the collar never bacons at the tip, and an organic-cotton pitch that was ahead of its time, and called it the Players Shirt. It runs in 100 per cent Peruvian pima today and still costs ninety-eight dollars.

The name comes from the sound of crickets, by the brand's own telling: the noise of being comfortably off-course. Criquet has never fully committed to being a golf brand. One half of the catalogue is Range Polos in brrr , a mineral-infused yarn that moves heat off the skin, and Players Shirts you could tee off in at Butler. The other half runs pearl snaps, fine-wale corduroy in burnt orange and a loop-terry shirt called Midnight Toker, which belongs on a pool deck more than a first tee. The two halves hang in the same closet.

Discmania, the Finnish house that supplies most of disc golf, printed the brand's mascot Carl onto a three-disc set. daphnes-headcovers.name: Daphne's Headcovers
daphnes-headcovers.line: Founded 1979 by Jane Spicer and her mother. Made Frank, the tiger headcover Tiger Woods carried.
src: The argument for this group is not who founded the brands but how well the things are made, and Jan Craig is the proof. In 1962 a golfer of that name, out on a rural route outside Cincinnati, made her own headcovers in worsted wool because she could not buy any she liked for a new set of clubs. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set within a few years, Tom Watson carried them, and so did multiple Ryder Cup teams. Every cover is still hand-knit to order, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver.

The animal headcover came seventeen years later, from a mother and daughter in Phoenix. Frank, the tiger, went on Tiger Woods' driver at the 1997 Masters, Nike licensed the character and named him, and the business grew four hundred per cent in a quarter.

Neither of those is a novelty company, and neither is interesting only for who started it. Seventeen brands do both things at once: founded or co-founded by a woman, and making what men buy, which is headcovers, leather, bags, gloves, towels, socks, polos and shoes. Almost every women-founded golf brand makes women's apparel and nothing else, and almost every independent brand making unisex hard goods was founded by men, so the overlap between the two runs thin.

devereux-golf.line: Scottsdale brothers, est. 2013, named after their grandfather — relaxed silhouettes before that was normal.
src: Robert Brunner studied geology at TCU, went to work in the gas industry, and hated it. He quit, spent a year at fashion school in Los Angeles, and came back with an idea for a golf line. He pitched his brother Will, who took on business operations. That was 2013.

They named it after their grandmother. Asked about it in the brand's first year, Robert didn't dress it up: "It's my grandmother's name. She turns 90 in March. We just named it after her, we wanted to keep it in the family. She still wears high heels to this day, she's a neat old lady."

The reason it exists is the same reason a lot of good brands exist, which is that the founder couldn't find what he wanted. "It all came from when I played, thinking, What can I wear?'" he said. "There's Puma, which is all flashy. I went through my Puma phase. The problem is that there's nothing that was fun on the course and off the course. Nothing for a night out." In 2013 that was a real gap. Golf shirts were boxy, mass produced, and cut for nobody.

What's striking about going back to that interview is how little the technical brief has moved. Robert named three details then that Devereux is still building around now: a slightly smaller spread collar that stays out of the way through the swing, a placket thinned down so it lies flat, and a fit shaped around how men are actually built. Add a smaller chest pocket and you have described the Homestead and the Phoenician, twelve years later.

edel-golf.line: David Edel fitted putters by where you actually aim, measured with a mirror and a laser. He sold the company in 2023; the method outlived him.
src: The good Texas golf brands are makers rather than marketers — a silversmith, a knitter, a pair of machine shops — which is the reason to run them together. The bar is narrow on purpose: founded in Texas, and still based in Texas. That cuts the brands putting a longhorn on a hat from an office in California, and it cuts the companies that opened a Dallas warehouse and started calling themselves Texan.

Sixteen clear it, and they have startlingly little in common. Clint Orms has been hand-engraving silver in Kerrville since 1992 and will not reproduce more than ten pieces from any one design. Ally Aiken painted a course map for her husband in 2020 and now has hundreds of courses in the catalogue. Harry and Zach wrap leather grips in Conroe as a father-and-son shop, Scott Matthews left investment banking in New York for Dallas over a polyester polo, and Mike Taylor and John Hatfield came off the Nike payroll on a Friday and opened Artisan in the same Fort Worth building on the Monday.

That last one is the closest thing to a pattern. When Nike left the golf equipment business in 2016 it left behind a ten-thousand-square-foot building in Fort Worth and a group of people who knew how to grind a wedge, and two of the best club shops in the country grew out of the vacancy. P53 leases its space in that same building from Marty Leonard, whose father Marvin built Colonial. Ben Hogan is buried in the city. The metal work clusters where it does for a reason.

One distinction matters in the apparel section: designed in Texas and made in Texas are not the same claim. Criquet designs at its Clubhouse in Austin and prints made in Peru on the Players Shirt. Artisan prints made in Fort Worth on the building. Both are fine, and the good ones say which is which on the product page.

fella-golf.name: Fella Golf
fella-golf.line: Tongue-in-cheek European golf — heavyweight tees, a pizza-slice ball marker, zero seriousness.
src: Fella Golf is an Amsterdam-based label registered as Fella Golf B.V. and built on a single line: "for the ones already too far gone. It only takes one good shot." That slogan runs through everything they make — from rib knit polos and cashmere vests to pizza-themed headcovers and ball markers stamped with the motto. The S/S '26 collection just dropped, and it covers the full spectrum: polos, tees, knitwear, outerwear, headwear, bags, and playful accessories that refuse to take the game too seriously.

What sets Fella apart is the range. A 190 cotton-cashmere golf cart intarsia crewneck sits next to a 15 golden pizza slice ball marker. A limited collab with Portland's Jones Sports Co on bags shares shelf space with a "Sandbagger" graphic tee and a bucket hat called the Cha-Cheng. The brand transcends golf from course to everyday wear — streetwear boldness meets traditional golf aesthetics, Dutch design meets global ambition. If you've been looking for the European answer to the indie golf wave, Fella is already too far gone.

forden-golf.name: Forden Golf
forden-golf.line: Streetwear-leaning golf label. The Swingman logo comes from Doc Edgerton's 1938 strobe photograph of a swing at MIT.
src: Forden Golf makes clothes for municipal golf, and it is specific about it. The graphics are in-jokes about the local muni, the scorecard and the putt you left short. The cuts are boxy cotton and heavyweight fleece rather than anything technical. The whole range runs from fourteen dollars to seventy-seven. None of it is trying to get you through the gate at a club that would ask what you shot.

The reference points are skate graphics and mid-century sports print, and the logo tells you which one the brand takes seriously. Forden calls the mark the Swingman, and it comes from Harold Edgerton's strobe photography at MIT in 1938: a golfer dissolved into fifty superimposed selves, the shaft still bending after the ball has gone. Flattened to one colour on a hat panel, the figure keeps what made the original work. It is a picture of motion rather than a picture of a golfer.

Chad Gurman founded the brand and has kept the brief narrow. "Forden Golf was founded on the belief that golf fashion should be as dynamic and expressive as the game itself. Our mission is to provide a wardrobe that effortlessly blends the elegance of the sport with the boldness of street style," Gurman says on the brand's own site. In practice that means cotton fleece, boxy tees, type-led graphics about municipal golf, and a hat line made with New Era.

Who it is for: the golfer who walks nine after work, keeps a cheap towel clipped to the bag, and would rather look like they came from somewhere than from a pro shop. The tee packet is the entry point at fourteen dollars, the New Era caps are the piece that will outlast the trend, and the sweatshirts are what you will actually wear off the course.

found-golf.name: Found Golf
found-golf.line: Half gallery, half golf label — Melbourne's Lance Peach and Ellen Keillar sell paintings next to polos.
src: Melbourne's Found Golf treats the course like a studio and the dress code like a memo it never received. Fashion-first golf from a city that already knows how to blend streetwear with fine art.

The Box Par Tee is the entry point — a heavyweight graphic shirt that reads like an art-school print, not tournament merch. The Daisy Chain Tee runs the same energy. The Reusable Ciggie Box is actually a tee holder, which is the most Found Golf thing imaginable. Dad cap in olive and The Shiz Vest round out a tight five-piece lineup. Everything priced in AUD, shipped from Australia, but the aesthetic is universal: golf gear for people who went to art school.

fyfe-golf.name: Fyfe Golf
fyfe-golf.line: Harris Tweed and tartan headcovers made to order in Fife — plus RAF flight suits and Augusta coveralls cut into covers.
src: Fyfe Golf makes headcovers to order in a workshop in Fife, out of Harris Tweed, Scottish tartan, waxed canvas from Dundee and, several times a year, something that used to be a completely different object — an RAF flight suit, a caddie's coverall from Augusta, a deck chair, a bolt of sail cloth off a yacht on the west coast. Thirty-two pieces are below, twenty-three of them headcovers, all in stock on 14 September 2026.

The brand started with a complaint. Neil Rennie had spent years walking into Scottish pro shops and finding nothing in them that had anything to do with Scotland. "Going around the pro shops and golf retailers, I couldn't find that more elevated product, with heritage and provenance," he told The Wandering Golfers in 2022. "Everything was mass-produced and heavily branded." He had come out of fashion rather than golf, which meant he already knew who still wove cloth in Scotland and how to reach them. Fyfe launched in November 2021.

If you want the short version: the Harris Tweed covers are the reason to know the brand, the tartans are the ones people ask about, and the reclaimed-material projects are where it gets interesting — and where almost everything sells out inside a week.
Twelve Harris Tweed cloths are in stock today. This is the heart of the range and the reason to know the brand.

gamut-golf.name: Gamut Golf
gamut-golf.line: One-of-one headcovers cut from vintage jerseys and course towels, plus hardwood alignment sticks.
src: Gamut Golf makes driver headcovers out of things that already existed. The baseball covers are cut from authentic vintage jerseys, several of them marked 1 of 1. The course covers are cut from genuine course towels — Shinnecock, Pebble Beach, the Old Course, Sawgrass, Pinehurst. Alongside those sit hardwood alignment sticks at $98, a solid brass divot tool, waxed canvas pouches and a set of walnut brushes.

The idea is not new — repurposing salvaged cloth into golf goods has been done before — but the sourcing is unusually specific. A cover built from a Mirage Cooperstown Collection throwback carries a team name that was retired decades ago, on fabric that was licensed when it was sewn in the 1990s. A Muirfield Village cover is lined with deadstock Ralph Lauren suit liner. The Richard Pouch uses rare deadstock Double RL. Each object is a second life for something, and because the input is finite, most of the interesting pieces are one of one.
For anyone who has looked at a rack of printed headcovers and wanted something with provenance, this is the catalog to read. It is also small — 35 products, most of them sold out most of the time.

The jerseys. Five covers are cut from authentic baseball jerseys: Cleveland Indians, White Sox, Pittsburgh Pirates, and two Mirage Cooperstown Collection throwbacks — the 1951 New York Giants and the 1957 Milwaukee Braves. Mirage produced officially licensed Cooperstown reissues in the 1990s, so the garments carried licensed marks when they were made. Gamut is cutting finished goods into new ones rather than printing logos, which is a different act entirely. Several are marked 1/1 for the obvious reason: one jersey yields one cover.

gramicci.name: Gramicci
gramicci.line: Climbing pants born on Yosemite granite in 1982 that quietly became golf-course staples.
src: Gramicci started in 1982 when rock climber Mike Graham needed pants that could handle big-wall climbs without restricting movement. The integrated webbing belt, the gusseted crotch, the freedom-of-movement philosophy — it all started on the granite faces of Yosemite. Forty-plus years later, Gramicci makes everything from the original climbing pant to UPF-rated rashguards, and the brand has quietly become a favorite among golfers who walk munis in the summer heat. The same design principles that work on El Capitan — unrestricted range of motion, durable natural fabrics, easy-adjust fit — work just as well walking 18 in August.

The range runs from the $44 Nylon Gramicci Cap to the $170 Taos Canvas Jacket. Organic cotton twill, nylon-cotton blends with water-repellent finishes, UPF-Shield stretch fabric — Gramicci builds clothes for people who actually move. No logos screaming, no performance marketing jargon, just well-made pieces with real climbing DNA. Eighteen picks here that prove you don't need a golf brand to play great golf.

gray-haast.name: Gray + Haast
gray-haast.line: Named for the founder and the largest eagle that ever lived — clean Queensland golfwear.
src: Australia is the best golf destination almost no American has been to, and the problem is information rather than distance. Half of what gets written about the Melbourne Sandbelt in the US repeats a myth about Alister MacKenzie designing all of it, and almost none of it tells you what a trip costs or how you get on one.

Two things are going on down there. The independent apparel and leather brands have got very good very fast, and nobody outside Australia is covering them properly. Alongside them sits a small set of organised trips an American can book, with prices exactly as published and a clear note where an operator publishes none.

Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip, and no other golf media or apparel brand in the world does. The rest of the field sits it out: No Laying Up, Fried Egg, The Golfer's Journal, Bob Does Sports, Good Good, Skratch, and a dozen clothing labels from Manors to Malbon to Eastside. Fried Egg has a deposit system and a calendar published a year ahead, and points its entire international programme at Britain and Ireland. That leaves a hole in the market, and for now one fourteen-person van tour is filling it.

Brand prices are in Australian dollars, because that is what these businesses charge. At late-August 2026 rates an Australian dollar is about seventy-two US cents, so knock off a bit under a third. Trip prices are quoted in whatever currency the operator publishes, and each one is labelled. Where an operator publishes no price at all, that is noted rather than guessed at.

gumtree-golf.name: Gumtree Golf & Nature Club
gumtree-golf.line: Small-batch headcovers, bags and apparel sewn in a Greenpoint studio from upcycled and vintage textiles, by a Melbourne transplant who put the gum leaf in the name.
src: Gumtree Golf & Nature Club runs out of Brooklyn, and the Nature Club line is what happens when a brand that sews headcovers from wetsuit neoprene and runs three-day ecology retreats in the Catskills decides to make a full wardrobe. Sixteen pieces, almost everything handmade in New York City or Los Angeles. The materials read like a forager's haul: deadstock vintage cotton lace, Angora goat mohair, herringbone neoprene, 4-way stretch ripstop, Portuguese rigid denim.

Nothing here screams golf. No polos, no tech fabrics, no moisture-wicking marketing copy. Instead you get barrel jeans made in Portugal, cropped linen shirts with shell buttons, and a tank top with white-on-white embroidery. The headcovers and hats bridge the gap — wetsuit neoprene cut into driver covers, 5-panels stitched from ripstop and herringbone cotton. Two percent of every purchase goes toward pulling CO out of the atmosphere. Quantities are low. The deadstock lace shirt is down to its last unit.

huega-house.line: Carlsbad, est. 2022 — retro-modern prints, towels and objects that treat golf as graphic design.
src: The name comes from the Danish word hygge — the art of cherishing the little things. The spelling changed because Americans kept butchering the pronunciation, but the idea stuck. Jonathan Ruley, a 30-year-old marketer from Boise State, and Jake Ryan, the former Green Bay Packers linebacker who played 48 NFL games including five postseason, are future brothers-in-law who bonded over one shared frustration: they couldn't find a hat that fit right. So they split $10,000 and made their own.

That was 2022. By mid-2024, Huega House hit $2.3 million in annual revenue — profitable, no venture capital, fewer than ten employees. The growth came organically. Aaron Rodgers wore one on the Pat McAfee Show and at a Knicks playoff game. Shohei Ohtani, Josh Allen, Nick Bosa, and TJ Watt all started showing up in them. Nobody was paid. Golf Digest featured the brand. Jake Ryan does all the photography himself. The aesthetic pulls from 90s sports and automotive culture — vintage graphics, structured crowns, clean embroidery — and the result is headwear that reads equally well on the course, at the range, or walking the dog.

The line has grown beyond hats into performance tees, hybrid shorts, hoodies, crewnecks, and sweats. Everything runs $22 to $88. Based in Carlsbad, shipping worldwide, and building a community around their HH Run Club and ambassador program. No big-box retail. No paid endorsements. Just product that people keep coming back for.

Updated, August 2026: the machine keeps rolling. The range now runs from $14 beanies to performance packs, the Flow Running Hat gives the run-club crowd a course-ready option, and the drops keep selling through — most of the Legacy and Athletics colorways below are restocks of sellouts. The brand's Instagram tells the story best: hometown San Diego baseball graphics, studio campaigns, and the moodboard-on-a-wall design process, which is why we've added a proper In the Wild section below.

jlindeberg.name: J.Lindeberg
jlindeberg.line: Founded 1996. Put Jesper Parnevik in tight pink trousers and changed how golf dresses.
src: J.Lindeberg is the brand that made golf clothing fit, and it did it by dressing one Swede in trousers nobody else would wear. The label was founded in Stockholm in 1996 by Johan Lindeberg , who had spent the first half of the nineties building Diesel — first as its distributor in Sweden, later running the American business — and who arrived in golf with a fashion marketer's read on a sport that had stopped caring how it looked. Thirty years on, that founding argument has been so completely absorbed that it is hard to remember it was ever an argument.

The pitch was simple and slightly rude. Golf in the late eighties and early nineties had drifted into oversized polos, pleated slacks and beige, and Lindeberg thought the game had lost its own history. His reference points ran backwards rather than forwards — Walter Hagen's tailored knits, Arnold Palmer's pullovers, seventies silhouettes, Steve McQueen. He wanted golf to look like it had before it got comfortable.

To prove it he needed a player, and from the mid-nineties he had Jesper Parnevik . Parnevik gives him the credit without hedging: "Johan Lindeberg deserves a lot of the credit, though. When he first approached me, he had this idea to go back to the time when golfers dressed smart." On what came before, he is blunter — "Something happened in the '80s when all the clothes became XXXL in size, very loose and tacky." And on the first pair of trousers he was handed: "They were so tight I could hardly bend over to pick the ball out of the hole but I shot a 63, so I didn't really care."

The moment everything turned on is precisely dated. 14 May 2000, the GTE Byron Nelson Classic at TPC Las Colinas. Parnevik started the final round three shots back, and instead of warming up he changed his trousers and walked to the first tee in pink. He won on the third playoff hole, beating Davis Love III. The same day, he reached number seven in the world — the highest ranking any Swede had held. Lindeberg named the idea the Pink Strategy , and the brand has revived it as the campaign for its thirtieth year, which is why a pink trouser sits at the top of this page.

jones-sports-co.name: Jones Sports Co
jones-sports-co.line: The 1971 carry bag that never went away — revived in Portland and better than the original.
src: Jones makes the best carry bag in golf by leaving things off it — no legs, no cart strap, no panelling to break the surface — and has been doing that from Portland, Oregon since 1971. The founding story is better than most because it is small. George Jones was a forty-year-old taxi driver who sewed the first bags in his basement and sold them out of the trunk of his cab. Jones still tells it that way on their own history page, and finishes the thought with a line that is hard to improve on: "Who could have known? George Jones, that's who."

What their site skips is the middle. George sold the company in 1990, and the new owners tried to make a Jones bag compete with the big manufacturers by making it less like a Jones bag. By the early 2000s the brand was effectively gone. The Lemman family and Chris Carnahan bought it in 2011, and what they bought was almost nothing: no patterns, no inventory, no factory. Matt Lemman, asked later what came with the deal: "Just the name, that was all."

They reverse-engineered it from the bags that were still around Portland. Carnahan has said they gathered old ones from family and friends, and there were plenty to gather, because the bags last. They rebuilt to the original specifications in modern materials, which is why the Original still looks like the photographs from 1975 and weighs 2.9 lbs.

The current line runs from the $125 Original through the F-35 ripstop stand bags, the Rider cart bag, eighteen officially licensed school versions and the collaborations with PAYNTR, BEAMS and Lusso Cloud. One correction to something you will read elsewhere: Jones does not claim anywhere on its own site to have invented the single-strap carry bag.

juniper-james.name: Juniper & James
juniper-james.line: From the founder of Duck Camp, named for his twins — breathable polos for Hill Country heat.
src: The good Texas golf brands are makers rather than marketers — a silversmith, a knitter, a pair of machine shops — which is the reason to run them together. The bar is narrow on purpose: founded in Texas, and still based in Texas. That cuts the brands putting a longhorn on a hat from an office in California, and it cuts the companies that opened a Dallas warehouse and started calling themselves Texan.

Sixteen clear it, and they have startlingly little in common. Clint Orms has been hand-engraving silver in Kerrville since 1992 and will not reproduce more than ten pieces from any one design. Ally Aiken painted a course map for her husband in 2020 and now has hundreds of courses in the catalogue. Harry and Zach wrap leather grips in Conroe as a father-and-son shop, Scott Matthews left investment banking in New York for Dallas over a polyester polo, and Mike Taylor and John Hatfield came off the Nike payroll on a Friday and opened Artisan in the same Fort Worth building on the Monday.

That last one is the closest thing to a pattern. When Nike left the golf equipment business in 2016 it left behind a ten-thousand-square-foot building in Fort Worth and a group of people who knew how to grind a wedge, and two of the best club shops in the country grew out of the vacancy. P53 leases its space in that same building from Marty Leonard, whose father Marvin built Colonial. Ben Hogan is buried in the city. The metal work clusters where it does for a reason.

One distinction matters in the apparel section: designed in Texas and made in Texas are not the same claim. Criquet designs at its Clubhouse in Austin and prints made in Peru on the Players Shirt. Artisan prints made in Fort Worth on the building. Both are fine, and the good ones say which is which on the product page.

kingfisher-golf.name: Kingfisher Golf
kingfisher-golf.line: Started at a kitchen counter in East Dallas by a former PepsiCo art director; first athlete signed via a Worst Golfer in Dallas contest.
src: Kingfisher Golf comes out of Dallas by way of PepsiCo's creative department. Founder Fiona Cohen spent years as an art director specializing in animation and motion design before launching a golf label that treats apparel like a design project — not a merchandise run. The tees are screen-printed at Lewellyn's Print Shop in Old East Dallas. The polos are produced by the same factory teams behind the big-brand performance shirts you already own. Everything stays under $56.

The brand's breakout moment was the "Worst Golfer in Dallas" contest — a city-wide search for the most entertainingly bad golfer, covered by D Magazine and backed by a cream heavyweight tee that became the brand's fastest seller. The winner, Colin Perry, is now Kingfisher's first sponsored athlete. It's the kind of move that only works when a brand genuinely doesn't take itself too seriously. Heading into the second half of summer, the lineup has grown into a legitimate collection: patterned performance polos, boxy streetwear-cut tees, and a deep hat wall that covers every style from camo trucker to unstructured dad cap. Nothing flashy, nothing over-engineered — just Dallas golf energy with a design eye behind it.

Revisited, August 2026: Kingfisher had a moment this spring — D Magazine covered the "Worst Golfer in Dallas" contest, which ended with Colin Perry crowned as the brand's first sponsored athlete (prize: lessons and general glory). Since our first post, the whole catalog was repriced — polos now $65, tees $40, caps $36 — and the range roughly doubled: the Kit, Mechanic, Navy Zipper, and Cream polos below are new, along with the Golfmobile and Athletics tees and a DAL cap wall that now runs eight colorways deep. Prices updated throughout.
Kingfisher didn't start in a studio. It started at a kitchen counter in East Dallas, at the spot where Fiona usually sat with a sewing machine and a pile of thrift store fabric scraps.

lamb-crafted.line: A six-person Texas machine shop — engraved putters, markers and leather from Tyson Lamb's bench.

left-of-field-golf.name: Left of Field Golf
left-of-field-golf.line: Surf and skate silhouettes for the course, every collection named for a stretch of Australian coast.
src: Left of Field is the funniest brand in golf that also makes clothes you would wear without the joke attached. Nick Ilias has run it out of Sydney for four years, starting in 2022 in his brother's old bedroom, which he described in a journal entry written in Paris three years later as "a small room filled with everything from late-night brainstorming sessions to boxes stacked high with stock."

Ilias started from a complaint a lot of players will recognise. "When I first started playing the game, getting dressed for golf felt like a lose-lose situation. The outfits I wanted to wear made me feel out of place in the pro shop. Adhering to the dress code just didn't feel natural, either."

What he built is not, as it is often described, a brand about Australian landscapes. It is a brand about silhouette . The aim in their own words is clothing "inspired by the attitude and silhouettes of surf and skate apparel, with design touches golfers can appreciate as their own," and then, flatly: "Our mission isn't to create products that scream golf'." That is why the shorts are roomy and cut to sit just above the knee, and why the trousers are pleated and wide. The tees follow the same logic, mid-weight and closer to a skate shirt than a golf one.

The landscape part is real, but it operates one level down, in the naming. Every collection ties to a specific stretch of Australian coast and the products take their names from places inside it. Elements is Barnbougle in Tasmania, photographed on the same ground. SOUTH is the Mornington Peninsula. RNP is Royal National Park, south of Sydney. The earliest polos were named after beaches in Sydney Harbour, the one case where they said so outright: "the Clontarf and Nielsen, named after iconic beaches within Sydney Harbour."

mackem-golf.name: Mackem Golf
mackem-golf.line: Wool headcovers sewn in the Perth hills — bespoke work from football shirts and family tartan.
src: Australia is the best golf destination almost no American has been to, and the problem is information rather than distance. Half of what gets written about the Melbourne Sandbelt in the US repeats a myth about Alister MacKenzie designing all of it, and almost none of it tells you what a trip costs or how you get on one.

mackenzie.name: MacKenzie Golf Bags
mackenzie.line: Handmade carry bags since 1985 — and the maker behind collabs for Fyfe, Sugarloaf, Miura and Bandon Dunes.
src: MacKenzie is a golf brand whose name is a tribute rather than a founder, and the story is better than most origin myths: in 1985 the Oregon PGA Tour pro Peter Jacobsen and his brother David started building bags and named the company after Rick MacKenzie , the St Andrews caddie who used to carry double for them and who solved the problem by tipping both their staff bags into a single leather pencil bag. The first logo was a drawing lifted off his business card. Forty years later the workshop still makes one thing, still makes it by hand in Oregon, and has quietly become the maker other brands go to when they want an object rather than a product.

That is what this page is about. MacKenzie itself publishes almost nothing — no collaborations page, no archive, a blog that went dark between July 2020 and November 2025 — so the record of who it has built for lives scattered across two dozen partner storefronts, most of them sold out. We went and collected it. What comes back is a picture of a very small company with a very long order book: ten employees, seven of whom actually make bags , supplying Scotland, Japan, Bandon Dunes and the Walker Cup at the same time.

The house style is unusually consistent for something made in this many colourways. An eight-inch top, a single strap, one pocket if you are lucky, full grain leather in an upholstery weight around a millimetre thick, and waxed canvas from a finisher that has been treating cloth since the 1800s. Todd Rohrer, who revived the company in 2006 with what he described as one stitcher and a cell phone, put the brief plainly: "the MacKenzie mantra has always been simple, beautiful, useful." On the question of everything else the industry bolts onto a bag, he was blunter: "In essence, most of what isn't a sack on a sling in unnecessary."

Current chief executive Nic Mulflur is clear that the simplicity is the hard part. "There are north of 40 pieces involved in our bags," he told LINKS. "It looks simple, but there are a lot of steps to make a bag to the exacting specifications of our customers." He is also fairly relaxed about who this is and is not for: "It's not for everybody. But for some of us, there's an emotional attachment to our bags. It's like a romantic relationship."

malbon.name: Malbon Golf
malbon.line: Co-founded 2017 by Erica and Stephen Malbon. Started as an Instagram mood board.
src: The argument for this group is not who founded the brands but how well the things are made, and Jan Craig is the proof. In 1962 a golfer of that name, out on a rural route outside Cincinnati, made her own headcovers in worsted wool because she could not buy any she liked for a new set of clubs. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set within a few years, Tom Watson carried them, and so did multiple Ryder Cup teams. Every cover is still hand-knit to order, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver.

The animal headcover came seventeen years later, from a mother and daughter in Phoenix. Frank, the tiger, went on Tiger Woods' driver at the 1997 Masters, Nike licensed the character and named him, and the business grew four hundred per cent in a quarter.

Neither of those is a novelty company, and neither is interesting only for who started it. Seventeen brands do both things at once: founded or co-founded by a woman, and making what men buy, which is headcovers, leather, bags, gloves, towels, socks, polos and shoes. Almost every women-founded golf brand makes women's apparel and nothing else, and almost every independent brand making unisex hard goods was founded by men, so the overlap between the two runs thin.

One pattern turns up again and again. Megan Chisti co-founded Seamus, trained as the designer, rebuilt the headcover that started the company and still sews product, and there is no published quote from her anywhere. Gail Hanson co-founded Bluetross, and the first prototypes came off her inherited sewing machine; the biggest feature ever written about the company is headlined "the unlikely story of a man who quit his job to make leather headcovers." Neither brand is hiding anything, and both credit her plainly on their own About page. The voice just defaults to him. So every entry names the woman, and says plainly when she co-founded with a husband or a mother rather than rounding up.

manors.name: Manors Golf
manors.line: London, 2019. Launched against technical golf apparel, then relaunched as a technical golf brand in 2023.
src: Manors is a London golf label founded in 2019 by two school friends who could not find clothes they wanted to play in. Seven years on it sells Polartec polos, recycled technical trousers and quarter-zip mid-layers — which is remarkable mainly because the brand was built on the argument that none of that matters.

The founding pitch was explicit. Jojo Regan and Luke Davies had been playing together through the summer of 2018 dressed nothing like golfers, and concluded that the industry was solving a problem they did not have. Nick Watts joined as Fashion Director and pointed the aesthetic at golf's golden age — Palmer, Player, Nicklaus — under a line the brand still uses: personality before performance .

The brand went dark on social in spring 2023 and came back as a technical golf brand. What follows is who they were, what changed, the three collaborations that mark the arc, and what is actually hanging on the rail now — because the most interesting thing about the current range is that both halves of the argument are still on it.

Photography Manors Journal The clearest read on Manors is not the product page. It is the Journal — trips to Royal Dornoch, Machrihanish Dunes, Arizona and the Players, shot like a magazine rather than a catalogue. The clothes are on people who are playing badly in weather, which is the argument the brand has been making since 2019. All photography below is Manors' own.

merrill-golf.name: Merrill Golf
merrill-golf.line: A design venture through the lens of golf — acid-washed tees, heavyweight fleece and a flying duck.
src: Merrill Golf calls itself a design venture through the lens of golf, and that's not marketing language — it's a literal description of how the brand operates. No polos. No moisture-wicking polyester. Instead: acid-washed tees, heavyweight hoodies, five-panel caps, and a flying-duck logo that channels vintage Americana more than any country club.

The Target Practice Tee ($60) and Golf Company Tee ($55) are the entry points — graphic-heavy, built on premium blanks, designed to be worn as much off the course as on it. The Birds Dad Hat ($50) and Target Practice Zip Hoodie ($150) round out a tight catalog that feels more tackle shop than fairway. Merrill is making golf apparel for people who fish, hunt, and happen to play golf — and it turns out that audience is bigger than anyone expected.

Golfers who also fish and hunt. The aesthetic reads closer to a tackle shop than a fairway, and that audience has turned out larger than expected.

metalwood-studio.name: Metalwood Studio
metalwood-studio.line: Cole Young's LA studio mining Y2K tour aesthetics — the blueprint for modern golf nostalgia.
src: Metalwood Studio is what happens when skate graphics and indie brand culture crash into golf — and nobody apologizes for it. Based on medieval heraldry and industrial signage, the design language is unlike anything else in the space. The Tri-Metal Tee at $54 is the entry point. The Bomber Jacket at $228 and Mechanic Jacket at $278 are the statement pieces.

The Medieval Terry Polo, the World Class Zip Polo, the Madras Explorer Shirt — every piece looks like it was designed by someone who cares more about art direction than sell-through. That's the whole point, and it's working.

And the collab r sum is unmatched for a brand this size. Before adidas came calling, Metalwood had already put its name on a FootJoy golf sneaker, a KEEN footwear capsule, a Maxfli collection that leaned all the way into the golden-era nostalgia, a Garrett Leight eyewear collab, an exclusive capsule with American Express and Hypebeast, and — most recently — the Oakley Pro M Frame, the 90s tour staple reissued through Metalwood s lens in a friends-and-family run that had collectors refreshing their feeds. Almost none of it can be bought today, which is exactly the point.

Revisited, August 2026: the story got bigger. Founder Cole Young — Carlsbad kid, D1 golfer at Loyola Marymount, four years inside Malbon Golf before betting on himself — turned an Instagram moodboard of '90s golfers in pleated pants into a La Brea Avenue studio with a global cult following. 2026 is the adidas year: the MC70 golf shoe with deco-stitching pulled from 1970s football boots, and a Predator Sala sneaker rebuilt in shaggy suede that had a line down the block in January. Below: the current collection's best, the new-era collab pieces, and Metalwood in the wild — from the LA store to a Paris party with Oakley.

midiron.name: Midiron
midiron.line: Nine products, no founder named, everything shot at night on a floodlit par-three.
src: Midiron writes better product copy than anyone else in golf and will not tell you who is doing it. There is no founder name on the site, no photograph and no byline on any of the writing. On a product page for a sold-out cap, in lowercase and unsigned, is this:

"when i was 10, my grandad gave me a hand me down titleist cap because i didn't have one to wear when we played golf together. sure, it was nothing special to anyone else, but it meant everything to me."

They went and found vintage Titleist caps, had a Melbourne rework studio customise three of them, gave one away and sold the other two as one-offs. The gesture describes the whole operation: small, sentimental and gone before most people heard about it.

The brand is Australian, run out of Sydney, registered in August 2025 and put its first product up that December. In the eight months since it has released nine things across seven drops: six caps, mostly cotton twill on an unstructured five-panel with a strap back, two polos in a unisex boxy cut, and one headcover. Three are already sold out, and the FAQ is blunt about whether that changes: "Sometimes. Usually not."

mogshade.name: Mogshade
mogshade.line: Handmade Portuguese headcovers and towels, made to order on a three-week lead.
src: Mogshade makes golf headcovers by hand in Portugal, and the name tells you everything about the sensibility: it comes from an old English dialect word for the play of light and shadow — sun filtering through leaves onto the course. The whole operation runs on what the brand calls ethical circularity. Everything is made to order (current lead time is about three weeks), which means no overproduction, and the fabrics are natural, recycled, upcycled, offcut, or deadstock — including rescued wool from the Serra da Estrela mountain factories that anchors the Re.Weave and Churra collections. Every piece is slightly different because the fabric was never mass-produced; what you get is what's left from the loom.

Since we first covered them in June, the catalog has kept moving — small handmade batches sell out fast here, which is half the appeal. The Depeche Golf magazine collab dropped in August with a special-edition headcover. The wall art program is real now: hand-tufted wool posters of imagined holes and pin sheets that take eight weeks to make. There's an Ocean Bottle collab, sweats, and socks. And for American readers, the practical note: since June, US orders ship with import duties and customs fees already included.

The other thing that sets Mogshade apart is how much company it keeps. For a one-workshop operation, the collab sheet reads like a map of independent golf: an artist series with Fabricaal that turned headcovers into canvases, a capsule with IGG that sold through in weeks, Projeto Serra — a tribute to the brand's home mountains, down to the "Ovelha Preta" black-sheep cover — and an "On Set with Manors " edit curated with the London golfwear brand. Add the Depeche Golf magazine bundle, the Ocean Bottle, a Fiumani cap, and the early Parmore run that was capped at 50 pieces, and you get the picture: almost everything they touch disappears. There's also a custom-made program if you want a cover built to your spec from whatever's on the shelf that month.
Updated, August 2026 — we re-checked every piece below against the current catalog, pruned what's sold out, and added twelve new items from the workshop.

morning-people-clothiers.name: Morning People Clothiers
morning-people-clothiers.line: Designed in the USA, sewn in South Korea — early-tee-time clothes with a five-piece discipline.
src: Morning People Clothiers was built by former collegiate golfers who turned professional and kept asking the same question: why does golf apparel feel like it's made for a billboard instead of a round? Their answer is a five-piece collection that strips out the noise — no loud patterns, no synthetic sheen, no billowy silhouettes — and replaces it with fabric you actually want against your skin at 7 a.m.

The centerpiece is the Golforever Polo, a proprietary 3-fiber blend (cotton, polyester, spandex) developed with South Korean textile craftsmen. It feels like your favorite broken-in tee but performs like a technical layer — moisture-wicking, stretchy, breathable in the heat. Three colorways, a tailored fit, and a refined collar that sits flat without a fight. The hat line — four styles made by Imperial — rounds it out at $32 each, from a cotton dad cap to a performance lid with their "Pacer" saddle-shoe icon, a nod to the pace-of-play ethos baked into the brand's name.

Morning People’s centrepiece, made from a proprietary three-fibre blend of cotton, polyester and spandex developed with South Korean textile craftsmen. It is moisture-wicking, stretchy and breathable, with a tailored fit and a refined collar that sits flat. It costs $75 and comes in three colourways.

odd-ritual.name: Odd Ritual
odd-ritual.line: Born in Cape Town, named for the small habits before every shot — golf without the gatekeeping.
src: Odd Ritual Golf was born in Cape Town because the founders couldn't find a local golf brand that spoke to them. The culture felt stiff, narrow, exclusionary — a game wrapped in rules about who could play and what they had to wear to do it. So they built something different. Named after the small personal habits every golfer has before a shot — the waggle, the alignment check, the ball mark tap — Odd Ritual is what happens when golf culture gets rewritten from the Southern Hemisphere.

Three pillars drive the brand: Community ("be lekker"), Creativity ("different strokes for different folks"), and Craft ("sweat the small stuff"). Everything is locally designed and produced in South Africa. No outsourced production, no borrowed identity. The tagline is "a modern expression of heritage," and they mean it — heritage as in the game's traditions, modernized through a lens that doesn't ask permission to be at the table.

Revisited, August 2026: when we first covered Odd Ritual it was a polos-tees-and-caps brand. Collection 03 changes that. The new range is a full wardrobe — their first Pleated Daily Trouser in 235gsm cotton twill, The Caddie Jacket with washed cotton lining and brass press studs, pigment-washed heavyweight crewnecks, and a 1990s Heritage Polo in 200gsm pique with contrast nylon collar and cuffs. All of it shot on-model in their Cape Town studio, all of it still locally made. Prices now run from R 200 (~$11) for socks to R 3,200 (~$176) for the Caddie Jacket. Off the course, the brand keeps building: their own Odd Folk Invitational golf day, and a website good enough to win Awwwards Site of the Day. This is Cape Town golf culture, built for the course and the community around it.

The founders started it because they couldn't find a local golf brand that spoke to them — the culture around the game felt stiff, narrow, and exclusionary. Their answer is a brand built on the back of tradition for people who love the game but want to feel like themselves on the course. In their words: less rigid, more real.

olydoe.name: Olydoe
olydoe.line: An ex-banker's anti-polyester manifesto — Supima cotton polos, launched October 2025.
src: Scott Matthews was an investment banker in New York who couldn't find a cotton polo he wanted to wear on a golf course. So he quit finance, moved to Dallas, and built Olydoe — a brand founded on what he calls an "anti-polyester manifesto." Launched in October 2025, every piece is made from Supima cotton with hollow-core yarn technology that delivers performance without the plastic feel. Crafted in Los Angeles, shipped from Kansas City, hats finished by hand in Portland, Oregon.

The name comes from combining the stars on the Chicago flag and the Texas flag — a nod to Matthews growing up in rural Illinois and planting the brand in Dallas. The brand DNA runs deeper than fabrics: his grandmother owned a fabric store, his mother used to embroider polos for his youth golf team. Press has called Olydoe "the Buck Mason of golf," and LINKS Magazine named it one of seven under-the-radar brands to watch.

The product line is deliberately tight — three polos in different stripe patterns, a long-sleeve option, a pique polo, one tee, and three hats. At $30 to $115, the entire lineup sits in a price range that says the brand is serious about the product, not the markup. No synthetics, no filler SKUs, no noise. Just cotton that actually feels like cotton, on a golf course.

Olydoe is a golf apparel brand launched in October 2025 and based in Dallas, Texas. It was founded on what its creator calls an “anti-polyester manifesto” — every piece is made from Supima cotton with hollow-core yarn technology, intended to perform without the plastic hand-feel of synthetic golf shirts.

p53.name: P53 Irons

penta-golf.name: Penta Golf
penta-golf.line: Three unnamed friends from magazine publishing — golf clothes with an art department's eye.
src: Australia is the best golf destination almost no American has been to, and the problem is information rather than distance. Half of what gets written about the Melbourne Sandbelt in the US repeats a myth about Alister MacKenzie designing all of it, and almost none of it tells you what a trip costs or how you get on one.

Two things are going on down there. The independent apparel and leather brands have got very good very fast, and nobody outside Australia is covering them properly. Alongside them sits a small set of organised trips an American can book, with prices exactly as published and a clear note where an operator publishes none.

Random Golf Club runs an Australia trip, and no other golf media or apparel brand in the world does. That leaves a hole in the market, and for now one fourteen-person van tour is filling it.

Brand prices are in Australian dollars, because that is what these businesses charge. At late-August 2026 rates an Australian dollar is about seventy-two US cents, so knock off a bit under a third. Trip prices are quoted in whatever currency the operator publishes, and each one is labelled. Where an operator publishes no price at all, that is noted rather than guessed at.

piretti.line: Milled from solid billets since 2008 — heavier heads, 2.5 degrees of loft, no cast putters ever.

public-drip.line: Neil Tan rediscovered golf at Van Cortlandt Park in 2020 and built the label muni New York now wears — script-logo polos, pleated trousers and denim buckets, nothing over $170.
src: Neil Tan rediscovered golf at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx in 2020, and the result is Public Drip — a label built for the golfers who grew up on public courses, not private ones. Brooklyn-based, streetwear-rooted, and already making noise with a Hypebeast feature, a Cleeks GC collab, and a LINKS Magazine nod as one of 2026's brands to watch.

The lineup runs deep: Frequency and Up & Down polos at $100, Anywhere Pleated Pants at $170, Tech Shorts at $90, and a full accessories run with the "P" Script bucket hat, snapback, and putter cover. Nothing here costs more than $170, and everything looks like it came from a brand three times the size. Muni golf has a uniform now.

puma-golf.name: PUMA Golf
puma-golf.line: COBRA PUMA GOLF's apparel and footwear arm — and the big brand most willing to take a swing at a collab.
src: The second PUMA Golf and Realtree collection is the one where the camo stops reading as novelty and starts reading as a colourway you would wear off the course. Precision in the Wild is ten pieces, released on Monday, and the interesting part is how differently it behaves from the first one.

The first drop, in February 2025, was a spectacle. It ran in Realtree Edge, Deep Forest and Rickie Orange, and it arrived on Rickie Fowler head to toe on the Thursday of the WM Phoenix Open, the rowdiest stage in professional golf and chosen deliberately. The second arrived on a Monday in late August in Dusty Olive and Alpine Snow, with no tournament and no player attached to it.

What it has instead is a new pattern. Realtree Legacy was made for the company's fortieth anniversary, and it is the first pattern co-designed by founder Bill Jordan and his son Tyler. It takes the dark bark structure of the Original pattern and warms it into browns and warm greys where Original ran cool, with segmented bark lines and drop shadows doing the depth work. On the fleece vest it looks like a hunting layer. On the spikeless HELSINKI G runner it reads as a shoe you would keep on off the course.

PUMA has form here. The Volition America line has carried camo golf shirts for years in patriotic red, white and blue for Folds of Honor. Realtree gives PUMA the same visual language with outdoor-industry provenance behind it, which is the argument PUMA itself makes: plenty of golf brands have dabbled in camo without much of it meaning anything.

quiet-golf.name: Quiet Golf
quiet-golf.line: From the Museum of Peace & Quiet orbit — considered golf clothes with an owl crest and an adidas Samba collab.
src: Quiet Golf explained: founders Christion Lennon (Museum of Peace & Quiet) and Raul and Diego Diaz, the Costa Mesa flagship, the Old Tom Capital backing, the adidas Samba collab, and what's new in the collection. Based in Costa Mesa, California — flagship store at 2949 Randolph Ave — they built a brand around the idea that golf style should be considered, wearable, and part of a larger rhythm. The owl crest, the QG monogram, the pennant flag: every detail is intentional without being loud.

The range runs from Supima cotton polos made in Portugal to cashmere sweaters, linen trousers, corduroy jackets, and collaborations with Adidas, Seamus, and Smathers & Branson. Old Tom Capital backed them in 2024. Nordstrom, Revolve, and Shopbop carry the line. Eighteen pieces here — from the $25 incense holder to the $380 cashmere cardigan — that show what happens when golf apparel starts with taste instead of tech specs.

Updated, August 2026: since our first post the story got bigger — The Old Ghosts profiled the Costa Mesa flagship this spring, the brand closed a seed round led by Old Tom Capital while promising to protect "the pace," and the collection keeps deepening: the new Monterey Hoodie, Jagger active-pique polo, pleated shorts, and a cable-knit Montecito in bone are below, and the pennant driver cover is back in red. We've also refreshed every product link and added the brand in the wild from their Instagram.

Quiet Golf is a Southern California golf brand built on restraint — muted palettes, minimalist design, and the idea of golf as somewhere you go to disconnect. In the founders' words: less performance, more presence. The range runs from supima polos and cashmere knits to needlepoint belts and pennant headcovers.

radry-golf.name: Radry Golf
radry-golf.line: A Wisconsin artist whose logo is a bird in a bucket hat — est. 2018, drawn before it is stitched.
src: Tony Knapton explained it in an interview a few months after he started the brand, and it has been sitting in plain sight on every piece he has made since. "One eye in the logo is a circle (birdies) and one is a square (bogies) — to represent both sides of par and both sides to golf." The wave where the mouth should be is the up and down of a round. "Coming to terms spiritually with the game is never ending. The game will always put you in situations and scenarios that you'll have to figure out. That's the beauty of it."

He wanted a logo with a back story. "Something where if you wanted to dive deeper into my brand, you'd find some other layers you may not have known about." Nine years later most people wearing it still think it is a smiley face, which is either a failure of communication or the most patient piece of design in golf.

Knapton started Radry in Wisconsin around late 2018 and runs it out of Sheboygan now. Every hat, crewneck and headcover begins as one of his drawings. He does not confine himself to a lane: asked where the work comes from he listed 90s design, abstract art, pop culture, high fashion, music and humour, and added "I try not to put myself in a box artistically."

The other half of the operation is White Dot Market, where the original artwork lives. Open edition prints, limited editions, and originals up to $3,900 for a Streamsong Black Hole #18. The apparel funds the art and the art justifies the apparel, and the collab tee in the grid below has both logos on it.

random-golf-club.name: Random Golf Club
random-golf-club.line: Erik Anders Lang's community that became a brand — meetups, films, and the only Australia trip in golf media.
src: Erik Anders Lang's first round of golf was December 12, 2011. He was almost 30, a photographer and music video director who'd worked with David LaChapelle and directed for Pharrell. He didn't identify with what seemed to be a sport for conservative White guys. So in 2017, he and co-founder Evan Roosevelt created Random Golf Club — "The Global Community of Local Golfers" — and set out to change who golf is for.

The first meetup was Melbourne, 2018. Eleven strangers played ten holes and nobody wanted to leave. Now there are 30,000 active members across 140 worldwide chapters, a Mad Scramble Tour that sends 100 players down the same fairway in 40+ cities, Classics at bucket-list courses from Sweetens Cove to Cabot Citrus Farms, and international Majors in Japan, Iceland, Ireland, Scotland, and New Zealand. The randomness mechanic is the secret sauce — your ball determines who you stand near and talk to. It's a bit like dressing a salad and mixing it all up.

The media arm is as big as the community. The EAL Show podcast runs every Monday — 350+ episodes, completely unedited, focused on why people golf, not how. RGC Films has 300,000+ YouTube subscribers and produces The Breaking Series, where RGC members play major championship courses from the pros' tees. Adventures in Golf — Lang's flagship — has run 8+ seasons traveling from Mumbai slums to Tokyo private clubs to Compton Municipal.

The pro shop is an extension of the community, not the point of it. The ECCO BIOM H5 collab shoe was born from an Adventures in Golf episode at Nuuk Golf Club in Greenland. The Blank Canvas Carry Bags in waxed canvas are anti-establishment by design. The City Golf collection is streetwear for golfers who grab pizza after a round. HQ is in East Austin. The Austin Mad Scramble hits Onion Creek on September 5. This is community-first golf, and the community is already 30,000 deep.

read-the-green.name: Read The Green
read-the-green.line: New York energy, est. 1997 graphics — the '97 nylon pullover is the piece that went viral.
src: Read The Green started as three words shouted at a buddy who missed the pin on a miniature golf course. Four lifelong friends turned that inside joke into a full lifestyle brand — premium hats and apparel that move between the course and the city without trying too hard. Their Founder's Cap is the signature piece, a 5-panel corduroy snapback with embroidered details and a custom interior lining, but the clothing line has taken on a life of its own.

The '97 Vintage Pullover went viral and put RTG on the map — a lightweight nylon layer with rib-knit cuffs and a drawstring waist that works on the back nine or a Saturday morning coffee run. The Grounds Crew Jacket and Oversized Knit Sweater pushed the brand into premium territory, while the Varsity Crewneck and Club Tee keep things accessible. Cody Bellinger, Jasson Domínguez, and Lexie Hull all wear RTG, but the brand still feels like it belongs to the weekend golfer who cares about what they put on. That's the point.

The brand's signature piece: a 5-panel corduroy snapback with embroidered details and a custom interior lining. It's the hat that put RTG's hat program on the map.

rouqe-golf.line: Mock necks and retro rugby stripes, shot on a dry mountain course. Founder not publicly named.
src: Rouqe Golf does 1974 club-pro styling better than any label its size, and the proof is which pieces are missing. The burgundy and cream rugby stripe has sold out. So has the black long-sleeve with the cream chest banding, and so has the houndstooth. Twelve of the twenty-one pieces in the men's collection are gone, and the loudest ones went first, which tells you more about the brand than a fabric spec would.

What is left is a small and unusually coherent range. The mock neck is the silhouette everything is built on, cut in six colours at fifty-nine dollars, in a category where nearly everyone defaults to a three-button placket. Around it sit retro stripes and a palette of sage green, chocolate brown, burgundy and cream that runs across both lines. The brown mock neck and the brown skort are shot on the same couple, which is more coordination than most labels this size bother with.

The photography is the other thing. Rouqe shoots two ways: hard-lit studio portraits against black and deep maroon, styled closer to a streetwear campaign than a golf catalogue, and on-course work at golden hour on a dry mountain course with a lake in the middle distance. Every image on the site is the brand's own, and it carries more atmosphere than labels ten times the size manage.

What Rouqe will not tell you is who runs it. There is no About page, and the URL returns a 404. No founder is named on the store or in any interview, and the domain registration is privacy-shielded. The one person publicly attached to the brand is Marko Mijaljevic, its Head of Design, credited with the SS25 collection. The domain was registered in spring 2023, which dates the shopfront rather than the company. For a label whose whole pitch is a point of view, the anonymity is a strange choice, and the clothes are good enough that it is the only thing holding the story back.

royal-albartross.line: Luxury golf footwear made in Italy and Portugal, founded by designer Alex Bartholomew.
