seamus.name: Seamus Golf
seamus.line: Hand-cut wool headcovers and blacksmith-hammered markers from a Beaverton workshop that covered the 2016 U.S. Ryder Cup team.
src: Seamus turns the headcover into the most personal object in the bag, in registered Irish tartans and licensed Pendleton wool, and the company started with one that was falling apart. Akbar Chisti's father had given him a wool cover from a famous links club, Royal Troon by the company's own telling, and it had worn through. His wife Megan was a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills, so in 2011 she remade it from fabric remnants, sewed a few more for his golf group, and then the two of them were running a company out of their garage. It is named after their Irish Terrier, Seamus O'Reily, and you pronounce it SHAY-mus.

The first wholesale order came from Bandon Dunes, where Akbar had caddied in college. Fifteen years later the operation still cuts and sews everything in Beaverton, Oregon, in wool, leather, canvas and seersucker, with fabric from Pendleton and from UK mills including parliament-protected Harris Tweed. It wholesales to roughly 700 shops worldwide and the Chistis still own all of it.

Two things make Seamus more than a nice accessories company. The first is the 2016 Ryder Cup, when Matt Kuchar commissioned personalized American flag covers for the entire U.S. team: thirteen hand-cut stripes, fifty embroidered stars, each one sewn in Oregon. The second is the blacksmith. The Hand Forged line of markers, pitch tools and money clips is hammered rather than cast, by a smith in Portland who now does about ninety per cent of his business with Seamus. The USGA lets them set up and hammer markers on-site at U.S. Open merchandise pavilions, where the brand has sold every year since Chambers Bay in 2015.

The catalogue has three parts. Driver and fairway covers are the engine of the company, at $120 to $170. The putter shelf is where the fabric library shows off, in registered Irish tartans, Hawaiian barkcloth and licensed Pendleton patterns. The forged bench runs $36 to $76, and hand-stamped personalization on it is free.

sentinel-golf.name: Sentinel Golf
sentinel-golf.line: Minneapolis walker bags from $810 — Dyneema, Danish textiles, and no interest in compromise.
src: Sentinel Golf is a product design lab in Minneapolis that makes golf equipment the way an outdoor brand makes a tent. Founder John Mooty runs it on a limited pre-order model — a window opens, you buy or you miss it, and there are no restocks and no discounts — and spends the rest of his time convincing manufacturers outside the game to take a job in it. A Danish tannery. A Nashville chair company. A Brooklyn machine shop. Tent-pole engineers in South Korea. The catalog reads like a list of favors called in.

The reference point is not golf at all; it is the Boundary Waters, the million-acre stretch of protected Minnesota wilderness where you camp, canoe and fish all day with no cell service and can drink the water under your canoe. Mooty built the Basecamp series to hold that feeling inside a golf trip, and the second Basecamp capsule was shot at Sand Valley across three days of camping, fishing and golf on one itinerary. It is why the writer Michael Williams called Sentinel an American Snow Peak, but for golf.

Which makes it a brand for a fairly specific reader: the walker who cares where the fabric was woven, who would rather own four objects for a decade than forty for a season, and who is not put off by an eight-week wait or a bag that costs more than a driver. Prices run from a $30 sock to a $2,900 dome tent. The sold-out archive is longer than the live shop, and that is the point — 112 of the 196 things Sentinel has made are already gone.
Bags first. Sentinel started by rebuilding somebody else's masterpiece in materials nobody had brought to golf, and the carry line is still where the brand argues hardest.

siegelman-stable.name: Siegelman Stable
siegelman-stable.line: Max Siegelman's NYC stable — racing-heritage sweats that ended up on tour players and a Maxfli box.
src: Siegelman Stable started the way a lot of great brands do — with family history and $600. Max Siegelman's father, Robbie, founded Siegelman Racing Stable in 1982 and spent decades training harness racehorses. Robbie also created equine therapy programs for cancer patients at Hackensack Hospital and inner-city kids from Newark. When the pandemic shut everything down, Max printed hats stamped with the family's horse-and-sulky logo, shipped them to the NBA Bubble, and watched the brand take off from there.

The golf connection runs deeper than the Maxfli collab. Max's first job was caddying. The "Harness the Drive" collection with Maxfli is a 14-piece capsule that includes a golf polo, headcovers, an ivy hat, a pullover jacket, and track shorts — all built in the same heavyweight fabrics and intentional detailing that define the mainline. The standout piece is the Short Sleeve Harness Shirt: a charcoal button-up with a removable green harness strap that clips on with a metal swivel clasp. It's the kind of design element that makes you stop and look twice — harness racing hardware repurposed as fashion hardware, and it works on a golf course.

Beyond golf, Siegelman Stable has collaborated with the Knicks, Mets, Yankees, Rangers, Tottenham Hotspur, Prince Tennis, Ford, the Indy 500, Don Julio, and the Muhammad Ali Estate. A portion of all proceeds still goes to equine therapy programs — the same work Robbie started 40 years ago. This is a family-owned brand with substance behind the logo.
A New York clothing brand founded in 2020 by Max Siegelman, built around his family’s harness racing heritage. Prices run from $48 to $780.

P53 leases its space in that same building from Marty Leonard, whose father Marvin built Colonial. Ben Hogan is buried in the city. The metal work clusters where it does for a reason.

One distinction matters in the apparel section: designed in Texas and made in Texas are not the same claim. Criquet designs at its Clubhouse in Austin and prints made in Peru on the Players Shirt. Artisan prints made in Fort Worth on the building. Both are fine, and the good ones say which is which on the product page.

sinking-birdies.line: Bold-print Cabretta gloves, towels and covers. Co-founder Christina Rogers verified via Companies House.

students-golf.name: Students Golf
students-golf.line: Campus-inflected golfwear built on varsity graphics and a deep bench of collabs.
src: Students Golf doesn't look like any other golf brand — and that's the point. Founded in 2022 under the tagline For Golfers Who Study The Game,' the label filters streetwear, academic culture, and vintage Americana through a golf lens. Everything borrows from campus life: the Calculus pants, the Librarian polo, the 1st String sweater. Even the internal line is called Course Studies Division.' It's golf apparel designed by people who grew up on skate videos and college football Saturdays, not country club verandas.

The catalog runs deep — 500+ SKUs across polos, pants, shorts, outerwear, hats, headcovers, and accessories. We pulled 18 pieces that represent the full range of what Students does. The Calculus Baggy Pleated Pants are the signature — oversized, carabiner-clipped, built from a custom trico-rayon-spandex blend. The Librarian Polo anchors the performance side with micro-waffle texture and UV protection. The hats and headcovers round it out. Everything ships free in the U.S.

sugarloaf-social-club.name: Sugarloaf Social Club
sugarloaf-social-club.line: The group chat that became a brand — Ian Gilley's crew, est. 2011, sailing capsules and hidden gems.
src: Sugarloaf Social Club runs the widest price range in independent golf and holds a single point of view across all of it. The catalogue reaches from a MacKenzie sailcloth bag at $1,400 down to a paper fan at $14, and both read as the same company. It started as a group chat. A few college roommates were graduating in 2011 and wanted somewhere to keep talking about golf, so they named the thread after the course they had spent four years on. The chat became an annual trip, and the trip became an Instagram account that at one point had more followers than Golf Digest. Ian Gilley filed the LLC in 2017 and has described the sequence as "a happy little accident."

The course they named it after is dead. Sugarloaf Mountain in Minneola, Florida was Coore & Crenshaw's first design in the state, built in 2008 across more than 250 feet of elevation, and it opened directly into the financial crisis. It never recovered and it is permanently closed. A brand named after a course you can no longer play is an on-the-nose metaphor for how golf nostalgia works, and to their credit SSC has never leaned on it.

Sugarloaf is a subsidiary of Pro Shop, Inc., the media company founded by Full Swing producer Chad Mumm and Joe Purzycki, which raised around $20 million from the PGA Tour and Powerhouse Capital and also owns Skratch and GolfWRX. Skratch discloses this in its own coverage. It explains how an independent-looking brand from McLean, Virginia ends up with an officially licensed THE PLAYERS capsule in the navy, gold and white it drew up for TPC Sawgrass.

The catalogue reads as thirty-three projects. MacKenzie bags built from retired sailcloth sit next to a $14 paper fan printed for a Japanese golf media brand, a teal-striped soccer kit made for a coffee bar, and a Western Golf Association line supporting the Evans Scholars program. Most of it has sold out.

sun-mountain.name: Sun Mountain
sun-mountain.line: Invented the modern stand bag in 1986 and the folding push cart in 1999; still assembles its bags in Montana.
src: Sun Mountain invented the bag with legs, and four decades on it still makes the lightest way to walk a golf course. In 1981 a club pro named Rick Reimers quit his job in Northern California and got in the car to drive north to Montana, to ski and think. The car radio was broken, so he spent the whole drive designing a golf bag in his head. What came out the other end was a nylon carry bag that weighed less than half what the leather and vinyl bags of the day weighed.

That was the BACK 9, and it was more interesting than it was successful. The FRONT 9 arrived in 1984 with a moulded top and bottom, sold properly, and became the shape every other carry bag copied. It also earned Sun Mountain the job of building the L8 bag for Ping, which put a Missoula startup in the position of manufacturing for one of golf's giants.

Then, in 1986, they put legs on it. The Eclipse is the bag Sun Mountain is credited with inventing, and its patented stand mechanism is now hinged onto almost every carry bag in the game. They ran the same trick twice more. The Speed Cart in 1999 folded down small enough that people bought one, and a walking-cart category appeared where there had not been one. The ClubGlider in 2008 put retractable legs on a travel bag, so an airport stopped being a workout.

Here is the part that gets left out. Reimers ran the company for 41 years as founder, director and sole shareholder, with no partners, no investors and no board. In March 2022 he sold Sun Mountain Sports to Solace Capital Partners, a Los Angeles private equity firm, and kept the scooter business. The bags are still assembled in Missoula, which remains unusual for the category. The fabrics come from Asia, and the company says "assembled in the USA" rather than made, which is the honest version.

swag-golf.name: Swag Golf
swag-golf.line: Painted headcovers and putter covers, and a 62-piece licensed college program across fifteen schools.
src: On 25 August, Swag Golf published sixty-two licensed college pieces in a single day — fairway covers, driver covers, desk caddies and six miniature tour-bag coolers, spread across fifteen schools. It is the largest licensed run any brand in our universe has put out at once, and it landed the week college football started.

What makes it more than a logo exercise is the naming. Almost nothing here is called the Texas Cover or the Georgia Cover. They are called Hook 'Em, Between The Hedges, Hoo Hoo Hoosiers, Get Out Of Our Swamp, Walk Of Champions, OH-IO, Geaux Tigers. Swag licensed the marks and then went looking for what the student section actually shouts, which is a harder brief and a much better one.

Austin five pieces Texas gets the deepest run in the program — a driver cover, two fairway covers, a desk caddy and one of the six coolers. It is also the one that moved fastest: the Longhorns cooler was already out of stock when we pulled the catalogue on 2 September, eight days after the program went up.

Six schools $222.22 The strangest object in the program and the one that explains it. Each is a scaled-down staff bag — hood, pockets, school marks — that opens as a cooler. At $222.22 they are more than twice the price of anything else here, and five of the six are still in stock.

takomo-golf.name: Takomo Golf
takomo-golf.line: Finnish direct-to-consumer irons, est. 2021 — tour-quality forgings at half the shop price.
src: Takomo launched in 2021 out of Turku, Finland with a premise that shouldn't be radical but somehow still is: forged irons, clean design, half the price. No pro shop markup, no retail middlemen, no tour-van mythology. They design the clubs, partner with top-tier foundries, and ship direct. The savings go straight to the price tag — a full set of S20C forged cavity backs for $649, when comparable Japanese-forged sets from Mizuno or Srixon run well north of a thousand.

The lineup spans every skill level. The 101 MKII is a hollow-body game-improvement iron that won MyGolfSpy's Best GI Iron — serious forgiveness at $579 for a seven-piece set. The 201T MKII, new for 2026, is a players precision iron aimed at better ball strikers who want workability without giving up distance. And the 301 CB is the crown jewel: single-billet S20C carbon steel, forged and finished with the kind of feel you associate with boutique Japanese smithing, not a DTC brand that also sells $15 gloves. Wesley Bryan played Takomo irons on the PGA Tour. The Skyforger wedge, at $99, uses the same 8620 steel alloy that Cleveland and Vokey charge nearly double for.

The Scandinavian design DNA shows up everywhere — minimal branding, matte finishes, clean toplines. No loud graphics, no oversized cavities screaming for attention. Takomo makes the case that the traditional equipment pricing model is broken, and then they prove it by shipping clubs that perform alongside irons three times their price. If you haven't heard of them yet, you will.

Takomo spent its first years as an irons company. The 101, the 201 and the 301 covered game improvement through to blades, all forged, all sold direct out of Turku at prices that undercut the houses making comparable heads. That remains the centre of the business.

twentyfour-golf.name: TwentyFour Golf
twentyfour-golf.line: Small-batch Australian covers and accessories, twelve pieces at a time.
src: TwentyFour Golf is a Gold Coast label that sells golf caps, and then a few clothes. That is not a slight — it is the shape of the catalogue. Eighteen of its twenty-four products are hats, and the six garments sit on top of a cap line that is almost permanently sold out.

It started with one product. The OG Camo Cap went live on 1/15/25, and the digital camo on it has since become the closest thing the brand has to a signature, turning up on a thermal and a second cap colourway. The business behind it registered in Australia in July 2024, runs out of a PO box in Currumbin on the southern Gold Coast, and ships worldwide in Australian dollars.

The brand writes about itself in the first person and never signs its name. Its vision page says golf "shouldn't be bound by rigid traditions. Instead, it should embrace individuality, creativity, and fun" and describes a range "born on the sun-drenched east coast of Australia" reflecting "the laid-back lifestyle I love." That is the whole of the origin story as published.
Eleven of the twenty-four pieces can still be bought as of 9/15/26. Sizes noted where they have gone.

walker-golf-things.name: Walker Golf Things
walker-golf-things.line: Pro skater Jack Fardell's label — named after Nicklaus, collabs with adidas, Wahine and Coopers.
src: Walker Golf Things draw everything by hand, and Blooming Grounds is the fullest expression of that they have put out. Walker are Australian, which is what makes the drop land oddly and also makes it interesting. It went live on 21 August as an ode to spring, to the opening rounds of the season and the flora along the fairways. In Melbourne that is exactly right. In Austin it lands in the back half of an August sitting at a hundred degrees.

Read it as a forward buy rather than a right-now one. The seersucker shirt and the Featherlite polo work in Austin immediately, the fleece hood is a December purchase, and the rest sit somewhere in between.
The collection runs to six pieces, $50 to $120, in sizes S through XXXL. One of them matters more than the rest: the knit polo has an entire landscape knitted into the body.

The distinction is a real one. Most graphic golf shirts are a print sitting on top of a finished garment. Walker built the artwork into the structure of the fabric instead, as a jacquard, where the picture is made out of the yarn itself. It costs more and it takes longer, and it separates a shirt with a picture on it from a shirt that is the picture. The same scene appears on the tee, and there it is a print, and the two sitting side by side make the point better than any description does.
